Base any translation-quality judgement on prior linguistic and contextual analysis, description, and explanation before making value or appropriateness claims.
Evaluate translations as linguistic-textual recontextualizations whose quality depends on both observable textual choices and socio-cultural/situational context.
Do not use translationese indicators as a direct proxy for translation quality; quality judgments need separate evidence for meaning preservation and pragmatic acceptability.
Keep translation’s double orientation visible by checking both fidelity to the prior source event and fit with target-language genre and reception expectations.
Treat equivalence as approximate value across differences, assessed at text level and prioritized case by case across denotative, connotative, pragmatic, text-normative, and formal-aesthetic demands.
Reject global impressionistic or contradictory assessment criteria unless they are converted into explicit, operationally checkable textual and contextual tests.
Do not accept target-only, reception-only, or response-only evaluations as sufficient when they cannot explain the source-translation relation or distinguish translation from adaptation.
Require any purpose-oriented TQA method to define textual function explicitly, identify source-text type, compare translation methods or shifts, and evaluate adequacy against text-specific features.
Ground socio-political, ethical, or power-focused critique in detailed linguistic analysis of forms and functions before drawing macro-level conclusions.
Integrate social-contextual and cognitive perspectives as complements, while keeping the assessment anchored in the textual evidence available for the source and target texts.
Treat usage norms, reader-response data, market response, and judge samples as insufficient unless their empirical basis and operational procedure are explicit.
Separate obligatory system-driven shifts from optional translator choices before assigning evaluative responsibility for a translation difference.
Reject analytic category sets that overlap, lack theoretical grounding, obscure text-context relations, or make target-language evidence inaccessible to evaluators.
Use argumentation structure as a useful comparison lens only when it fits the source genre, and do not let it displace other linguistic or micro-textual features.
Assess meaning preservation across semantic, pragmatic, and textual dimensions rather than reducing equivalence to referential content.
Analyze translations as discourse utterances whose illocutionary force depends on context, not as isolated sentence correspondences.
Build the quality comparison from a detailed source-text profile that specifies the function to be sought in the target text.
Use the source-text profile as the quality norm and compare the target text with the same dimensions and level of delicacy.
Define text function as use in a particular situational and cultural context, not as a direct projection from broad language-function typologies.
Break context into manageable situational dimensions and inspect medium, participation, social role, and social attitude through linguistic evidence.
Use micro-, macro-, and superstructural levels to judge error seriousness only as part of a specified, text-context-sensitive procedure.
Assess seriousness by mismatch patterns and affected functional components, not by raw error counts or isolated referential mistakes.
Analyze style and province as functional evidence by checking shared background, implicitness, formality, institutional convention, domain activity, topic, and production details.
Treat text function as realized through situational dimensions and their syntactic, lexical, and textual correlates.
Include textual devices in the analysis by tracking theme dynamics, clausal linkage, iconic linkage, deictic dependence, and overall text organization.
Classify mismatches as covert functional errors when dimensional profile differences alter function despite acceptable grammar or denotation.
Classify overt errors separately as denotative omissions, additions, substitutions, wrong selections or combinations, ungrammaticality, and questionable acceptability.
Weight errors by their effect on the individual text’s ideational and interpersonal functional match rather than by a universal error hierarchy.
State the assumptions and exceptions behind dimensional error judgements, including cultural comparability, intertranslatability, and whether the target has an added special function.
Allow analyst judgement only as argued, evidence-constrained hypotheses, acknowledging that equivalence and TQA retain non-absolute and subjective elements.
Treat poetic-aesthetic sources and foregrounding according to whether form is detachable from meaning and whether foregrounding serves expression itself or communicative effect.
Use linguistic cues such as spoken-mode absence, passivization, pronouns, requests, modality, and questions to diagnose medium, participation, and social-role effects.
Inspect pronouns, agency, passives, non-human subjects, syntactic markedness, information order, and text sequencing as evidence of interpersonal strategy.

Use formal-style and province markers such as complex noun phrases, complete clauses, formal lexis, technical terminology, explicit alternatives, dating, figurative absence, and cohesion to characterize function.
Synthesize function by stating how marked dimensions contribute to ideational and interpersonal components, recognizing that one device may serve both.

Treat preservation of factual content as insufficient when target choices weaken addressee involvement, flattery, reassurance, indirectness, responsibility management, hedging, or interpersonal force.
Classify a case as overt translation when the source’s historical occasion, source-culture status, or aesthetic identity prevents direct source-function replication for target readers.

For overt translation, aim at second-level access to the source function, preserve the source as intact as possible, and balance necessary explanation against replacement of source-culture markedness.
For overt translation, preserve equivalence at language/text, register, and genre levels while giving target readers second-level access to the source function and cultural impact.
Classify a case as covert translation when source and target addressees have comparable contemporary needs and the target can function as an original in its own culture.
Apply a cultural filter in covert translation only for verified target-culture presuppositions, and default to cultural compatibility when difference is unproven.
For covert translation, account for target pragmatics through cultural filters supported by multi-method research on register and genre variation across language pairs.
Classify unjustified cultural-filter changes as covert versions, and classify added special-audience or special-purpose renderings as overt versions rather than ordinary translations.
Require empirical contrastive-pragmatic support before treating covert target-text changes as legitimate cultural filtering.
Decide translation type from source status, use, reception history, purpose, and brief, not from source-text features alone.
Limit claims of full functional equivalence to covert translation, with special scrutiny of interpersonal components because they depend on culturally variable role and attitude norms.
Default to cultural compatibility in covert translation unless language-pair evidence supports differences in norms such as directness, content focus, explicitness, or routine reliance.
When evaluating covert translation, check whether titles, advertising, signs, or other target texts reveal shifts between explicit content, interpersonal address, directness, and implicitness.
Weight errors by source-profile priorities, evaluation objective, and functional component, treating denotative mismatches as especially serious when ideational function is central.
Measure revised-model quality by analogous source and target profile/function analysis while distinguishing dimensional from non-dimensional mismatches.
Build register analysis from Field, Tenor, and Mode: lexical granularity and subject matter; participant relations and stance; channel, participation, and oral-literate dimensions.
Use Genre to connect individual texts to macro-contextual text classes and combine it with language/text and register to characterize textual function.
Analyze translation as frame and discourse-world movement, then choose criticism criteria according to whether the sought function is overt or covert.
For covert translation, permit language/text and register manipulation only when it preserves target-frame genre and individual textual function.
Keep source-target comparison in the assessment even when target-audience appropriateness or translation purpose influences whether the product is a translation or version.
Treat overt dialect or provenance transfer as partly subjective when contrastive ethnographic status evidence is unavailable.

Discover genre from everyday lingua-cultural practice, expect translation to remain in the source genre, and route null target-genre realizations to version or non-verbal alternatives when covert equivalence is desired.
Interpret genre-convention change through multiple hypotheses: translation mediation, globalization reflection, and translator conservation of target norms.
Use genre-level corpus comparison to relate an individual text pair to norms and options in that genre and language pair.
For children’s picture books, analyze whether lexis, syntax, cohesion, iconic linkage, sound patterning, and repetition support young listeners’ comprehension, drama, and involvement.
In children’s books, treat respect for readers and characters, naming, titles, conversational rituals, reassurance, and gentle socialization as core Tenor and genre-function evidence.
Evaluate title, ending, added material, and framing changes as functional shifts when they move a children’s text away from its source atmosphere or role relationships.
Flag translations that normalize imaginative agency, over-simplify capable-reader syntax, or alter address and action descriptions in ways that infantilize characters or impose hierarchy.
Do not assume children require domestication; consider overt access to foreignness or the original voice when covert adaptation substantially changes source function.
Ground cultural-filter decisions in language-pair empirical research on communicative preferences, values, and expectations.
Keep cultural-filter judgements current with language-pair developments because empirical evidence reduces arbitrariness but communicative norms continue to change.
Triangulate contrastive pragmatic evidence using elicited tasks, retrospective data, meta-pragmatic judgements, naturalistic data, and varied authority/familiarity relations.
Analyze discourse openings, closings, supportive strategies, gambits, requests, complaints, directness, politeness, roles, rights, and obligations when diagnosing pragmatic differences.

Treat German-English pragmatic differences such as directness, content orientation, self-reference, routine use, and explicit justification as corpus- and study-bound tendencies rather than fixed national traits.
Reduce stereotyping risk by testing contrastive findings against larger samples, bicultural expert interpretation, and multicultural comparison.
Analyze translation as intercultural communication without reducing culture to race, nation, region, etiquette, fixed mentality, or national character.
Treat language, knowledge, norms, culture, translator cognition, and social constraints as interrelated, situated phenomena when explaining translation choices.
Frame cultural explanation around who makes culture relevant to whom, for what purpose, where, and in which context.
Treat functional equivalence as a matter of intercultural understanding: a linguistic-cultural transposition that enables comparable function in a different context.
Account for translation’s double transmission and rupture by analyzing how texts are recontextualized across time, space, indexical orders, and language-cultural barriers.
Use translation’s reflective nature to surface ethical and intercultural implications while keeping the focus on situated text-context analysis.
Analyze globalized discourse across lexical, semantic, pragmatic-discourse, socio-semiotic, micro-process, and macro-process levels.
Evaluate borrowings and English imports by their contextual function, including whether they threaten local resources, facilitate communication, develop new functions, or signal identity.
Under globalization, test whether transported forms retain source function or acquire new local value through orders of indexicality and local uptake.
Treat globalized text production as negotiation and accommodation within hybrid cultures rather than as one-way transfer.
Evaluate ELF communication by mutual intelligibility, efficiency, and multilingual multicompetence rather than by native-speaker correctness alone.
Do not treat ELF as a threat that makes translation obsolete; check the complementary roles of ELF, native languages, translation, and localization in the domain.
Set translation quality requirements from the commission purpose and risk level, distinguishing basic understanding or information uses from publication, image, legal, or high-stakes uses.
Allow non-mother-tongue translation only with appropriate competence and controls such as qualified native-language revision or stylistic advice when target-native expectations matter.
Watch for under-researched English influence at syntactic, pragmatic, discourse, and textualization levels because these changes can be harder to detect than lexical borrowing.
Revise overt/covert expectations when current corpus evidence shows reduced cultural filtering, dominant English source-norm takeover, or emerging overt-like hybrid translation types.
Use carefully designed, contextualized parallel and comparable corpora to generalize and verify equivalence claims beyond individual cases.
Use corpora as one tool within a broader evidence set that also includes introspection, observation, textual analysis, and ethnographic analysis.
Combine qualitative and quantitative inquiry by using corpus statistics as prompts for recontextualized interpretation rather than as final answers.
Do not ignore low-frequency corpus findings when they illuminate translation function or quality.
Let a controlled TQA model supply qualitative categories before quantification, especially to reduce stereotype-producing corpus interpretations.
Use corpus comparison to examine addressee involvement, perspective, subjectivity, information organization, interactionality, and source-language shining-through.
Normalize corpus frequencies when subcorpora differ in size, and do not infer translation influence from frequency alone when item functions differ.
Use cognitive translation research to inform TQA only where it clarifies comprehension, transfer, problem solving, decision making, reconstitution, and bilingual pragmatics.
Use cognitive insights to enrich text-based TQA without replacing source-target comparison or making the individual translator the central quality object.
Treat verbal reports, behavioural process measures, and neuroimaging as limited evidence that cannot by itself establish underlying cognition or translation quality.
Account for different cognitive demands in overt and covert translation: overt co-activates source and target pragmatics, while covert primarily activates target pragmatics.
Recognize that expert translators may use either conceptual processing or more direct transcoding, so process assumptions should be evidence-based rather than presumed.
Treat frequency-based evidence of explicitation or simplification as product evidence unless the study design directly supports claims about translator process.
Avoid permanent cultural-filter generalizations; reassess each case against current communicative norms, globalization, internal diversification, and corpus evidence.
Use the updated Field/Tenor/Mode split to reduce category overlap: Field for lexis and processes, Tenor for stance and relations, Mode for medium, theme-rheme, coherence, and cohesion.
Assess mission statements as both exposition and exhortation, with special attention to corporate values and indirect requests for employee alignment.

In Field analysis of mission statements, inspect evaluative lexis, cliché collocations, intensification, subjective force, and process types that foreground beliefs or relations over material actions.

In Tenor analysis of mission statements, inspect missionizing stance, optimism, inclusive pronouns, persuasive positivity, grammatical metaphor, omitted agents, and accessible versus specialist terminology.
In Mode analysis of mission statements, distinguish oral-rhetorical writtenness from plain information delivery and evaluate repetition, parallelism, rhetorical macrostructure, and summative closure.
Use genre corpus evidence to check whether a single mission-statement analysis reflects broader target-culture genre norms.
When evaluating translated mission statements, check for shifts in positivity, emotional engagement, indirectness, rhetorical cohesion, perlocutionary effect, and genre interpretation.

Flag lexical and process shifts that weaken persuasive function, including negative shadow meanings, false friends, added material-action focus, specialist terminology, and loss of colloquial accessibility.
Flag Tenor shifts that turn positive missionizing into conditions, effort, discipline, direct request, exhortation, or pressure on addressee behaviour.
Do not treat local cohesion as sufficient when translation loses source macrostructural parallelism, rhetorical guidance, oral-rhetorical effect, or summative closure.
Treat cultural filtering as quality-relevant when target-culture directness, explicitness, and content orientation submerge rhetorical strategies central to source function.

Keep the revised model source-target comparative, with Participation under Tenor, process types under Field, textual aspects under Mode, connectivity covering coherence and cohesion, and corpus support for Genre.
Separate linguistic analysis from social judgement: textual profile comparison, description, and explanation ground evaluation but do not by themselves settle every good/bad judgement.
Account for social, political, ethical, publishing, marketing, reader, and purpose factors without letting them displace linguistic-textual analysis.
Use the overt/covert cline and translation/version distinction to state which linkage and textual operation are being evaluated.
Use House’s metalanguage to explain how and why translated texts differ from originals before arguing adequacy.

Treat translated text as an object of study in its own right — a genuine communicative event to be described on its own terms — rather than as a defective copy to be justified or dismissed against its source text.
Do not exclude translated text from a corpus on the assumption that it is inferior, contrived, or unrepresentative; translated text is a legitimate object of linguistic study.

Adopt a target-orientation: analyse a translation as belonging to the target textual system and treat the source text as a source of information or stimulus, not as the fixed standard the translation must meet; do not let equivalence or faithfulness to the source be the sole evaluative frame.

Make a coherent corpus of translated texts — not an individual translation or a single source-target pair — the primary unit of analysis in descriptive translation study, so that findings rest on many texts of the same type rather than isolated instances.

Treat the primary purpose of corpus work in translation studies as explaining what translation is — identifying the features of translated text that reveal how it works — not merely improving human or machine translation output; expect more reliable practical answers to follow once the phenomenon is explained in its own terms.

Identify translational norms descriptively and only from a corpus: a norm is a strategy translators repeatedly prefer over available alternatives in a given culture, observable solely through a representative body of translated texts — never deduced from the source text, the target system, or a general collection of target texts.

Ground translation theory empirically: induce generalisations from actual translated texts in function, and be sceptical of theories developed deductively or supported only by a corpus used to illustrate rather than to test them; remember that studies of context, and especially of usage, are feasible only with access to substantial amounts of real data.

Require a descriptive branch with an explicit, reproducible methodology: individual findings must be expressible as generalisations about translational behaviour, and the studies must be intersubjective and repeatable on the same or another corpus — a collection of case studies or comparative analyses alone does not qualify.

Model translation as a mediated communicative event: the activity of translating and the need to communicate through translated utterances is itself a major constraint that produces patterns specific to translated text, some of which cannot be explained by interference from the source or target language alone.

Define a universal feature of translation as one that typically occurs in translated rather than original text and is not the result of interference from specific linguistic systems, and treat any proposed universal as a candidate hypothesis to be tested, not an established law — the known evidence rests on small-scale studies and casual observation and its universality is assumed pending further research.

When analysing translated text, probe for the recurring candidate universals — a rise in explicitness (explicitation), disambiguation and simplification, a preference for conventional grammaticality, avoidance of source-text repetition, exaggeration of target-language features, and a distinctive distribution of common features — as hypotheses to be measured against evidence, without presuming any of them holds in a given corpus.
Treat translation universals as operational hypotheses about patterns and regularities, not as absolute laws.

To isolate a translation universal, assemble a corpus of texts translated into one target language from a variety of source languages, keep the patterns that recur across source languages and that are absent or rarer in original target-language text, and cross-validate against corpora of texts translated into other target languages before claiming the pattern is universal.

Keep universals and norms distinct: universal features arise from constraints inherent in the translation process and are taken to be culture-invariant, whereas norms occur consistently only within a particular socio-cultural and historical context and vary noticeably across languages and cultures — do not generalise a culture-specific norm into a universal.

Investigate operational norms through the corpus at two levels: matricial norms, covering omissions, additions, substitutions, and transpositions in the distribution of linguistic material, and textual norms, covering verbal formulation such as collocation choice, treatment of speech, and title conventions; expect their content to differ by language, culture, and period.

Distinguish the third code from translationese: the third code is a systematic distribution of features arising inherently from the confrontation of source and target codes and distinguishes a translation from both source and original target texts, whereas translationese is an artefact of a translator's inexperience or lack of competence in the target language — do not attribute a systemic pattern to individual incompetence or vice versa.

Choose the corpus type by the question: use parallel corpora (source texts together with their translations) to investigate equivalence and alignment, and use comparable corpora (comparable original texts across several languages) to investigate the nature and limits of equivalence and cross-linguistic feature contrasts; both are now supported by dedicated tools.

Choose the corpus design by the evidence needed: monolingual controls for target-language norms, comparable corpora for non-aligned contrast, parallel corpora for source-target comparison, and single translational corpora for translated-language specificity.

Use large computerised corpora to open questions that small-scale studies cannot settle — the intermediate stages of translation and how a translation evolves over time, the size and nature of the unit of translation, and the type and level of equivalence actually achieved in practice.

Preserve the strength of the evidence: report tentative, small-sample, or attributed findings as tentative, and never upgrade a hedged or candidate claim (for example a proposed universal or a predicted impact) into a categorical rule; match the certainty of a stated conclusion to the certainty of its support.
Study translated texts as target-culture language evidence in their own right before judging them by source-text equivalence.
Explain translated-text features through target-culture norms, conventions, and historical systems rather than reducing them to source-text derivation.
Frame corpus-based translation studies around explicit hypotheses, varied data, descriptive categories, and a methodology that can support both inductive and deductive questions.
Use explicitly designed machine-readable corpora together with suitable software tools; corpus evidence is only useful when it can be searched, counted, displayed, and analysed.
Treat corpus research as an empirical check on intuition; prefer natural-discourse evidence when claims about language patterning are disputed or assumed.
Match the corpus measure to the research question and control for its limitations before comparing texts.
Connect fine-grained textual measurements with cultural, ideological, pedagogical, and technological context when interpreting corpus findings.
Treat distinctive translated-language profiles non-evaluatively unless evidence shows actual incompetence or error.
Scope proposed translation universals as tendencies and test whether language-pair or culture-specific explanations fit better.
Use target-reader need, lexical availability, and meaning criticality to choose among superordinates, approximation, common synonyms, circumlocution, paraphrase, glossing, or loan-word retention.

Analyse simplification and conventionalisation through observable shifts such as title simplification, clearer syntax, shorter units, regularised punctuation, reduced repetition, and conventional collocation or dialogue formatting.
Make corpus design criteria, hypotheses, corpus type, and feature definitions explicit before testing claims about translated language.
Evaluate claims about stage suitability, speakability, or accessibility by comparing translated texts with corpus features that match the claimed function.
Check comparability, metadata, copyright clearance, and alignment requirements before attributing corpus differences to translation status or using parallel-corpus evidence.
Operationalise explicitation, simplification, and normalisation as distinct measurable constructs instead of treating them as interchangeable labels.
Interpret additions and omissions as functional translation strategies only after checking clarity, coherence, aesthetic intent, complexity, and whether omitted meaning is vital.
Generalise simplification hypotheses only after testing across genres, language pairs, and interpreted texts rather than relying on early or single-design evidence.
Test accessibility or audience-fit claims with quantifiable textual features and reformulate specialised content when the target audience requires it.
When adapting register-analysis tools to translation, analyse co-occurring feature clusters against an appropriate baseline rather than isolated feature counts.
Account for target-system norms and source-text status when interpreting normalisation, because these pressures can increase or reduce conventionalising shifts.
Attribute a pattern to an individual translator only after testing author style, source-language preferences, and sociolect norms as alternative explanations.
Use diachronic translational corpora to study how Bible translations change in orthography, phonology, morphology, syntax, lexis, register, terminology, and consistency over time.
Use corpus-based tools in Bible translation to describe existing translations, explain their systemic conditions, and support quality, accessibility, and skopos-specific decisions.
Use keyword, concordance, and collocation analysis to investigate cultural or ideological meanings in translated texts, but treat limited findings as hypotheses for further testing.
Include socio-cultural context in causal explanations of translational patterns instead of relying on linguistic counts alone.

Use corpus metadata to separate regional variation, dialect, source-language interference, translator-mother-tongue effects, institutional profile, team structure, target language, and source-text variants.
Preserve and document translation corpora as reusable research infrastructure so later studies can build on present analyses.

Ground corpus-based translation and interpreting advice in empirical corpus evidence, using quantitative patterns together with qualitative interpretation rather than treating either as sufficient alone.
Before selecting features or evidence, classify the study target as a general universal, a mediator-specific style, or a source-text response, then choose measurements that match that target.

For complex variation in translation or interpreting, discourage explanation from isolated frequencies or concordances and recommend multifactorial modelling when multiple explanatory variables are plausible.

When surveying Russian translation and interpreting corpora, include the Russian research tradition rather than assuming the field is represented only by better-known English, French, German, or Spanish work.
Select Russian translation corpora by aligning genre, register, access mode, annotation, size, and technical requirements with the study question and intended users.
For Russian interpreting research, treat corpus availability as a design constraint: expect scarcity, fragmentation, missing historical data, and no default Europarl Russian component.
When recommending Russian interpreting data sources, describe UN Web TV, SIREN, and COINCOUT with their acquisition, transcription, size, domain, and access limitations.

When evaluating universals or strategies, check patterns across lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels and avoid strong Russian interpreting generalizations until independent corpora replicate them.
In mode or producer comparisons, operationalize linguistic markers clearly and pair descriptive indicators with significance testing and effect sizes before interpreting group differences.
Treat English-to-Russian translationese findings as pair-specific until tested in other language pairs, especially typologically closer Slavic pairs.
Encourage Russian translationese studies to move beyond newspapers by using larger corpora and feature sets spanning lexical, morphological, syntactic, and genre-sensitive evidence.

For Russian translation and interpreting variation, model register and constrained-communication variables with morphological, syntactic, textual, proficiency, setting, medium, and audience metadata rather than relying on translation status alone.

Prioritize corpus construction and study designs for underexplored Russian varieties, especially constrained communication, amateur translation, post-edited translation, second-language translation, translator qualifications, and non-English language pairs.

Recommend supervised or unsupervised machine learning for Russian translation/interpreting only when the corpus is large, feature-rich, and metadata-suitable, and frame the result as pattern detection or classification rather than automatic explanation.
For advanced computational or process-oriented Russian corpus research, encourage interdisciplinary collaboration across linguistic, literary, computational, NLP, and psychological expertise.

For Polish-Russian or Russian-Polish multifactorial studies, require metadata-rich corpora that record factors such as translation direction, delivery mode, and text variety before making explanatory claims.
For ordinary Chinese prose, preserve concision, flexible syntax, and rhythmic force; resist Europeanized wording when it makes the sentence needlessly complex or stiff.
Use established Chinese idioms as live resources, not as decorative substitutes for thought, and do not flatten them into wordy paraphrase when the idiom fits.
Prefer concrete subjects, people, and event clauses over abstract nominalized subjects when revising Chinese sentences influenced by English syntax.
Replace weak-verb plus abstract-noun constructions with direct Chinese verbs whenever the phrase only repackages a plain action.
Do not use pseudo-technical abstract nouns merely to sound objective or elevated; revise to direct adjectives, nouns, or everyday expressions when precision does not improve.
Avoid redundant plural marking in Chinese when quantity words, collective nouns, or context already make plurality clear.
Avoid imported one-of and as-one-of structures when class membership is obvious; recast the sentence so the main subject is not buried under a heavy membership phrase.
Let coordinate Chinese words or phrases stand by juxtaposition when natural, and choose connectors that match progression, contrast, or adjustment instead of defaulting to English-like and-linking.
Delete topic and prepositional wrappers such as concerning, regarding, among, or in/on when the object or topic is clear without them.
Avoid over-explicit causal scaffolding in Chinese; remove formal because/therefore markers when sequence and context already convey the relation, and do not use a because-clause as the subject.
Do not force Chinese idiomatic verb phrases into stiff adverbial forms, and delete empty success adverbs when the verb already entails completion.
Reduce mechanical modifier-particle chains by deleting needless particles, using parallel or connective phrasing, or restoring verb clauses so modifier hierarchy stays clear.
Use postposed descriptive clauses for long modifiers so the head noun appears early and the sentence can expand naturally.
Rely on Chinese aspect words, time adverbs, and context to express temporal sequence instead of importing tense-like verbosity.
Prefer active or agentive Chinese constructions over imported passive patterns, and when passive meaning is needed choose an idiomatic passive expression suited to the event and register.
Distinguish ordinary prose correction from deliberate literary innovation: critique departures from norm only after checking whether the writer understands and knowingly varies normal Chinese idiom.
